newsitem.title: POLAND: WARSAW SHARE SURGE SEEN DRIVEN BY NEW FOREIGN FUNDS.
newsitem.headline: WARSAW SHARE SURGE SEEN DRIVEN BY NEW FOREIGN FUNDS.

text.p: The Warsaw bourse set third straight 33-month high, leaping well above the psychological barrier of 16,000 points on Thursday and analysts saw the buoyant foreign investor mood pushing shares to more records.

Analysts said Warsaw stayed in tune with worldwide bullish mood but were wary of making any predictions on how far the start-of-the-year investor optimism would take the Warsaw market before it hits a substantial profit-taking correction.

"We shouldn't talk about resistances at the moment, there is an uptrend and it's impossible to predict how far the market would go, what's important is that we've passed the psychological barrier," said Jan Koch of PBR SA brokerage.

They said the growth was fuelled by foreign investors opening new positions in the beginning of the year and the entry of new funds, lured by last year's 90 percent surge in local currency, which still saw some upside potential here.

The Warsaw bourse gained 23 percent since mid-December and its all-share WIG index closed at 16,341.2 points on Thursday, but analysts said such a steep rise could not go on forever even though it was hard to predict when the surge loses steam.

"It's not Polish investors who had moved the market, there is interest of foreign funds, but certainly there are limits above which it doesn't pay to go," said Jacek Dzierwa, an analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.

Analysts that the market had to go through some profit-taking corrections and consolidation periods after such strong gains but said investors' apparent indifference to fundamentals made the market largely unpredictable.

"It's difficult to say how long it (the rise) would last, the situation might change rapidly although I wouldn't expect it in the next few days," said Pawel Tarnowski, an analyst at Raiffeisen Capital and Investment Polska. He added that some foreign investors were already finding Polish stocks, now trading at 16.2 times historical earnings, overvalued and eyed Latin America for cheaper picks.
But they still considered Polish stocks as a better buy than emerging Asian issues.
Sonja Shechter, an analyst at Daiwa Institute said what made Polish stocks especially attractive was East Europe's and Poland's in particular potential for fast economic expansion.

"I think certainly at the end of last year the relative value was still quite good in Poland, but there are a couple of aspects which make me perhaps a little bit cautious, say, looking past the first quarter," she said.
She said forthcoming parliamentary elections due in the last quarter and large privatisations could cool investor sentiment.

Analysts say such offerings as the copper-giant KGHM Polska Miedz SA and Bank Handlowy SA, estimated at up to $1 billion and a planned private placement of Poland's biggest insurer PZU SA could divert substantial funds from the bourse.
They say Eventually large offers should help the bourse by boosting its capitalisation now at about 28 billion zlotys and drawing bigger funds, but that would be a long-term effect.
Some analysts said a possible rate-rise in the United States, likely to drag down major exchanges, could also have an psychological impact on the Warsaw market.
But Daiwa's Shechter said she still saw the market rising to at least 17,000-17,500 points by the end of the year.
